issues.legal_issue: A limited estate held by a Hindu woman under a bequest for her maintenance is enlarged into absolute ownership when the applicable succession law so provides.
material_facts: The owner’s will gave the woman property for her maintenance and restricted her power to alienate it, with the property to revert to his daughter after the woman’s death.
The woman held the property when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
She later sold and gifted property, and the appellant sought possession on the basis of the will’s reversionary provision.
issues.conclusion: Section 14(1) enlarged the woman’s limited interest into absolute ownership, so the will’s restriction and reversionary provision did not entitle the appellant to possession of the property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a limited interest held by a Hindu woman in property acquired in recognition of her right to maintenance is enlarged into an absolute estate. The Court applied V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddy, which held that a woman in a similar position became absolute owner of the property.

predicates.possession_case: The dispute is a suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.woman_possessed_property_when_succession: The Hindu woman held the property when the relevant succession law took effect.
predicates.property_given_for_maintenance: The property was given to the woman in recognition of her right to maintenance.

issues.definition: When a possession suit concerns property held by a Hindu woman under a maintenance-related grant at the time the succession law took effect, her limited interest is enlarged into absolute ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A prior declaratory decree does not bar a challenge under res judicata in a later possession suit when the decree is contrary to the law applicable to its legality or was granted without jurisdiction, unless a special enactment protects it.
material_facts: The appellant obtained two final decrees declaring that alienations by the woman would not affect the appellant’s reversionary rights.
The appellant later brought a suit for possession relying on those decrees.
The law declared in V. Tulasamma applied to the woman’s interest and made her the absolute owner, contrary to the basis of the earlier declarations.
No special enactment protected the earlier decrees in this case.
issues.conclusion: The earlier declarations did not bar the defendants from challenging their legality and could not by themselves support the appellant’s claim for possession; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not make a prior decision conclusive where it is contrary to the law applicable when its legality is reconsidered or where the court lacked jurisdiction, unless a special enactment preserves it. A declaratory decree simpliciter does not attain finality as a basis for a future possession decree if its legality can be challenged in that later proceeding. The Court relied on Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy, Chief Justice of Andhra Pradesh v. L.V.A. Dixitulu, Ashok Leyland Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Management of M/s. Sonepat Cooperative Sugar Mills Ltd. v. Ajit Singh. It also applied the reasoning in Balwant Singh v. Daulat Singh that a declaratory decree does not itself convey title to a reversioner. The Court did not decide the correctness of Teg Singh v. Charan Singh or Kesar Singh v. Sadhu, which involved a special enactment not applicable here.

predicates.possession_suit_based_on_prior_declarati: The plaintiff brought a suit for possession relying on an earlier declaratory decree.
predicates.prior_declaration_contrary_to_applicable: The earlier declaration conflicts with the law applicable when its legality is considered in the later proceeding.
predicates.prior_declaration_granted_without_jurisd: The court that granted the earlier declaration lacked jurisdiction to do so.
predicates.special_law_preserves_prior_declaration: A special enactment preserves the earlier declaration against the later challenge.

issues.definition: In a possession suit based on an earlier declaration, res judicata does not prevent a challenge to that declaration when it conflicts with applicable law or was granted without jurisdiction, unless a special law preserves it.
